WITH ordered AS (                      -- each pair's sends in time order
  SELECT invitation_id, sender_id, recipient_id, sent_at, status, status_at,
         LAG(sent_at) OVER (PARTITION BY sender_id, recipient_id
                            ORDER BY sent_at, invitation_id) AS prev_sent
  FROM invitations
), numbered AS (                       -- a running count of "this send starts a new invitation"
  SELECT *,
         SUM(CASE WHEN prev_sent IS NULL
                    OR sent_at > prev_sent + INTERVAL '{{resend_days}} days' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           OVER (PARTITION BY sender_id, recipient_id
                 ORDER BY sent_at, invitation_id) AS invite_no
  FROM ordered
), invites AS (                        -- one row per invitation: first send, latest send's outcome
  SELECT sender_id, recipient_id, invite_no,
         MIN(sent_at) AS first_sent,
         (ARRAY_AGG(status    ORDER BY sent_at DESC, invitation_id DESC))[1] AS outcome,
         (ARRAY_AGG(status_at ORDER BY sent_at DESC, invitation_id DESC))[1] AS outcome_at
  FROM numbered
  GROUP BY sender_id, recipient_id, invite_no
), placed AS (
  SELECT i.*,
         (SELECT mr.region
          FROM member_regions mr
          WHERE mr.member_id = i.sender_id AND mr.valid_from <= i.first_sent
          ORDER BY mr.valid_from DESC
          LIMIT 1) AS region
  FROM invites i
  WHERE i.outcome <> 'withdrawn'
)
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', first_sent)::date AS month,
       region,
       COUNT(*) AS invitations,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome = 'accepted'
                          AND outcome_at <= first_sent + INTERVAL '14 days') AS accepted_14d,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE outcome = 'accepted'
                                AND outcome_at <= first_sent + INTERVAL '14 days')::numeric
             / COUNT(*), 4) AS acceptance_rate
FROM placed
GROUP BY 1, 2
HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{min_invites}}
ORDER BY month, region;

Explanation. The grain the team wants is the invitation a member saw, not the send. LAG finds each pair's previous send; a send that is the pair's first, or more than the resend limit after the previous one, starts a new invitation, and a running SUM of that flag numbers them (classic gaps-and-islands). Each invitation keeps its first send (for the month and the start of the 14-day window) and the latest send's outcome. Withdrawn invitations are removed before anything is counted, so they affect neither the rate nor the floor. The region is looked up as of the first send. At Medium every row is its own invitation and the region table has one row per member, so the same query reduces to a filter and a grouped count.

Complexity. One sort by (sender, recipient, sent_at) for both window functions, a hash aggregate per invitation and one per (month, region); the correlated region lookup is an index probe per invitation with a (member_id, valid_from) key. O(n log n) overall.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake and BigQuery: QUALIFY is not needed here, but ARRAY_AGG(... ORDER BY ...)[1] becomes MAX_BY(status, sent_at) (Snowflake, Spark) or ARRAY_AGG(status ORDER BY sent_at DESC LIMIT 1)[OFFSET(0)] (BigQuery); COUNT_IF / COUNTIF replace FILTER; DATE_TRUNC(first_sent, MONTH) in BigQuery. An as-of region join can use Snowflake's ASOF JOIN … MATCH_CONDITION (first_sent >= valid_from). MySQL 8: window functions work; replace FILTER with SUM(CASE …) and the array trick with a ROW_NUMBER() subquery.

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: an invitation sent in the last minute of August and accepted in September (August); acceptances exactly 14 days after the send (counted) and 14 days plus one second (not); ignored, pending and withdrawn outcomes. Hard: resends after a withdrawal, including one sent exactly at the resend limit (same invitation) and later invitations to the same member one second past the limit (a new invitation); a resend crossing into September whose acceptance is late if measured from the resend; a lone sender in a small region exactly at the floor in August and one short in September. Very Hard: chains of three sends; two senders who move region, with an invitation starting exactly at the move (new region) and one started before the move and resent after it (old region).

Counting withdrawn invitations in the denominator; < instead of <= on the window; collapsing every send of a pair into one invitation regardless of the gap (or not collapsing at all); timing the window from the resend; using the first send's status instead of the latest send's; the sender's current region; applying the floor before removing withdrawals; integer division; DATE_TRUNC in a non-UTC session.

WITH ev AS (                           -- duplicate deliveries collapse to one event
  SELECT DISTINCT page_id, member_id, event_type, event_at
  FROM follow_events
), seq AS (
  SELECT *,
         LEAD(event_type) OVER w AS next_type, LEAD(event_at) OVER w AS next_at,
         LAG(event_type)  OVER w AS prev_type, LAG(event_at)  OVER w AS prev_at
  FROM ev
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY page_id, member_id ORDER BY event_at)
), counted AS (                        -- drop both halves of a quick unfollow-then-refollow
  SELECT page_id, event_type, event_at
  FROM seq
  WHERE NOT COALESCE(event_type = 'unfollow' AND next_type = 'follow'
                    AND next_at <= event_at + INTERVAL '7 days', false)
    AND NOT COALESCE(event_type = 'follow' AND prev_type = 'unfollow'
                    AND event_at <= prev_at + INTERVAL '7 days', false)
), eligible AS (                       -- the floor, on the count at the end of the window
  SELECT p.page_id
  FROM pages p
  LEFT JOIN ev e ON e.page_id = p.page_id
  GROUP BY p.page_id, p.followers_at_start
  HAVING p.followers_at_start
         + COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'follow')
         - COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'unfollow') >= {{min_followers}}
), weeks AS (
  SELECT (DATE '{{first_week}}' + 7 * g)::date AS week_start
  FROM generate_series(0, {{weeks}} - 1) AS g
)
SELECT e.page_id, w.week_start,
       COUNT(c.event_type) FILTER (WHERE c.event_type = 'follow')   AS follows,
       COUNT(c.event_type) FILTER (WHERE c.event_type = 'unfollow') AS unfollows,
       COUNT(c.event_type) FILTER (WHERE c.event_type = 'follow')
         - COUNT(c.event_type) FILTER (WHERE c.event_type = 'unfollow') AS net_new
FROM eligible e
CROSS JOIN weeks w
LEFT JOIN counted c
  ON c.page_id = e.page_id
 AND DATE_TRUNC('week', c.event_at)::date = w.week_start
GROUP BY e.page_id, w.week_start
ORDER BY e.page_id, w.week_start;

Explanation. Duplicates go first: the pairing below relies on each member's events alternating, and a duplicated follow breaks that. For each (page, member), an unfollow whose next event is a follow within 7 days is half of a round trip, and the follow whose previous event is such an unfollow is the other half; both are filtered out, so a round trip spanning a week boundary changes neither week. Because events alternate, each follow can only pair with the unfollow just before it, so two quick round trips in a row drop all four events. The floor uses the end-of-window count, which round trips do not change. The week spine is crossed with the eligible pages before the LEFT JOIN, and COUNT(c.event_type) counts only matched rows, so empty weeks come out as zeros.

Complexity. One sort per (page, member) for the window functions, a hash aggregate for the floor, and a join of the counted events to a tiny spine: O(n log n). In production the page-week counts would be maintained incrementally; see the follow-ups.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: DATE_TRUNC(DATE(event_at), WEEK(MONDAY)) (its default WEEK starts on Sunday), GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY(first_week, …, INTERVAL 7 DAY) with UNNEST, COUNTIF. Snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('week', …) follows the WEEK_START parameter (default Monday, ISO), a spine from GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => n) with SEQ4(), COUNT_IF. Spark SQL: date_trunc('week', …) is Monday-based; sequence() + explode for the spine. MySQL 8: a recursive CTE for the spine and SUM(CASE …) for the filters.

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: a quick round trip collapsed; pages above and below the floor; members whose first event is an unfollow (they followed before the window). Hard: refollows exactly 7 days after the unfollow (collapsed) and 7 days plus one second (both count); a round trip from late Sunday to Monday; follows at 23:59:59 on Sunday and 00:00:00 on Monday; a page that starts at or above the floor and ends below it. Very Hard: the same event delivered twice; two round trips in a row by one member; a page ending exactly at the floor (included).

Common mistakes. WHERE NOT (… AND next_type = 'follow' …) without COALESCE: for a member's last event next_type is NULL, the condition is NULL, and NOT NULL silently drops the row; not collapsing, or dropping only the unfollow; an exclusive 7-day bound; a self-join that pairs an unfollow with any later follow rather than the next event; omitting empty weeks; applying the floor at the start of the window; counting duplicates; Sunday-based weeks (a BigQuery habit).

Follow-up guidance. (1) Convert to the page's zone before truncating to the week; a Sunday 23:30 UTC event is Monday morning in Tokyo and moves weeks; the spine is then in local dates. (2) Publish with a "provisional" marker and restate the last two weeks when late events arrive; or publish weeks only after the lateness bound. (3) A longer window can collapse pairs whose halves fall in already published weeks; recompute the affected weeks, version the definition, and annotate the change. (4) Keep per (page, week) counters plus a small state of each member's last unfollow within the last 7 days; an arriving refollow inside the window decrements the unfollow's week instead of incrementing its own.

Rubric anchors. 2: weekly counts right but round trips not collapsed, or empty weeks missing. 3: matches the expected result at the level attempted. 4: also handles time zones, late data and incremental maintenance credibly.

Strong signals. Asks whether the floor applies at the start or end; states the alternation assumption and dedupes before relying on it. Red flags. Reporting which members unfollowed; treating every follow after an unfollow as part of a round trip regardless of time.

WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT message_id, seat_id, member_id, sent_at,
         LAG(sent_at) OVER (PARTITION BY seat_id, member_id
                            ORDER BY sent_at, message_id) AS prev_sent
  FROM messages
), grouped AS (                        -- a copy within the limit of the previous one joins its group
  SELECT *,
         SUM(CASE WHEN prev_sent IS NULL
                    OR sent_at > prev_sent + INTERVAL '{{dup_hours}} hours' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           OVER (PARTITION BY seat_id, member_id ORDER BY sent_at, message_id) AS grp
  FROM ordered
), kept AS (
  SELECT seat_id, member_id, grp, MIN(sent_at) AS kept_sent
  FROM grouped
  GROUP BY seat_id, member_id, grp
), first_response AS (                 -- the first response to any copy in the group
  SELECT g.seat_id, g.member_id, g.grp, MIN(e.event_at) AS responded_at
  FROM grouped g
  JOIN message_events e ON e.message_id = g.message_id
  WHERE e.event_type IN ('accepted', 'declined', 'replied')
  GROUP BY g.seat_id, g.member_id, g.grp
)
SELECT k.seat_id,
       COUNT(*) AS messages,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE f.responded_at <= k.kept_sent + INTERVAL '7 days') AS responses_7d,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE f.responded_at <= k.kept_sent + INTERVAL '7 days')::numeric
             / COUNT(*), 4) AS response_rate
FROM kept k
LEFT JOIN first_response f
  ON f.seat_id = k.seat_id AND f.member_id = k.member_id AND f.grp = k.grp
WHERE k.kept_sent + INTERVAL '7 days' <= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}'
GROUP BY k.seat_id
ORDER BY k.seat_id;

Explanation. The unit is the message a member received once, so copies are grouped first: per (seat, member) in time order, a copy more than the limit after the previous copy starts a new group, and a running SUM numbers the groups (chained, so three copies 5 hours apart under a 6-hour limit are one group). The group's earliest sent_at is the kept message. Response events are attached through every copy of the group and reduced to their MIN, so a decline on the first copy followed by a reply on the second is a response at the decline time. Messages whose 7-day window has not ended by the stated as-of time are left out, because they could still be answered. At Medium the copy and as-of rules are inert in the data, and the same query applies.

Complexity. One sort of messages by (seat, member, sent_at), a hash join of events to messages, two hash aggregates: O(n log n + e).

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake / BigQuery: COUNT_IF / COUNTIF; TIMESTAMPADD(HOUR, …) / TIMESTAMP_ADD(prev_sent, INTERVAL 6 HOUR); the gaps-and-islands pattern is the same. Spark SQL: sum(case …) over (…) and count_if; INTERVAL 6 HOURS. MySQL 8: prev_sent + INTERVAL 6 HOUR, SUM(CASE …) for the filtered counts.

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: duplicate pairs within the limit; reads without a response; a decline on the kept copy. Hard: a copy exactly at the limit (same group) answered on the copy; a copy one second past the limit (its own message); responses exactly 7 days after the send (counts) and 7 days plus one second (does not); a message sent exactly 7 days before the as-of time (counted) and later ones (left out). Very Hard: a chain of three copies spanning more than the limit from the first, answered on the third; a decline inside the window followed by a late reply on another copy.

Common mistakes. Counting read as a response or leaving out declined; deduplicating with DISTINCT member_id per seat (merges messages months apart); measuring duplicates from the first copy rather than the previous one; joining responses only to the kept copy; timing from the responding copy; using the latest response; filtering the as-of cutoff with NOW(); integer division.

(2) Keep a seat-assignment history with validity intervals and attribute each kept message to the recruiter holding the seat at kept_sent. (3) Compare response-time distributions by region and day of week; consider business-day windows, but state the definition change. (4) Maintain per-group state for the last 7 days (kept time, responded yet) and finalize a group once its window closes; daily aggregates are then append-only.

def skills_coverage(profiles, jobs, opted_out=None, min_count=None):
    off = opted_out or set()
    # Hard and above compare trimmed, case-insensitive names. At Medium every name is
    # already distinct and canonical, so normalising there changes nothing.
    norm = lambda s: s.strip().lower()

    n = len(profiles)
    nbytes = (n + 7) // 8
    rows = {}                                  # skill -> bytearray bitset of members
    counted = 0
    for i, skills in enumerate(profiles):
        if i in off:
            continue                           # opted-out members never enter the index
        counted += 1
        for s in {norm(x) for x in skills}:    # a skill listed twice is one skill
            buf = rows.get(s)
            if buf is None:
                buf = rows[s] = bytearray(nbytes)
            buf[i >> 3] |= 1 << (i & 7)
    bits = {s: int.from_bytes(buf, "little") for s, buf in rows.items()}
    size = {s: bin(b).count("1") for s, b in bits.items()}

    out = []
    for req in jobs:
        need = {norm(x) for x in req}
        if not need:
            c = counted                        # no requirements: every counted member
        else:
            acc = None
            for s in sorted(need, key=lambda s: size.get(s, 0)):   # rarest first
                b = bits.get(s, 0)
                acc = b if acc is None else acc & b
                if not acc:
                    break                      # nobody left
            c = bin(acc).count("1")
        if min_count is not None and c < min_count:
            c = -1                             # too few to show
        out.append(c)
    return out

Explanation. An inverted index from skill to members, built once, turns each job into an intersection of a few sets instead of a scan over every member. Bitsets make the intersection a handful of big-integer ANDs (each ~3 KB at 25 000 members) and the count a popcount. Building each bitset in a bytearray and converting once avoids the trap of bits |= 1 << i per member, which copies the whole integer every time. Opted-out members are skipped while building the index, so no later step can count them by mistake. Profile and job skills go through the same normalisation; requirements are a set. The minimum is applied to the final count, and 0 is below any positive minimum, so it is suppressed too.

At Medium the generated names are already canonical, so normalising is harmless; a candidate who compares exactly is equally correct there.

Complexity. Building: O(total listed skills) bit sets plus O(skills × members / 8) bytes. Each job: O(k × members / 64) word operations for k required skills, with an early exit. In the timing check the reference takes about 0.35 s in CPython; checking every member for every job (30 million subset tests) takes about 30 s.

Dialect notes. In Java, java.util.BitSet with and() and cardinality(); in production, compressed bitmaps (Roaring) keep sparse skills small and are what search and analytics engines use for this. In SQL the same count is a relational division: GROUP BY member HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT skill) = k over the required skills, per job. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. No members; a required skill nobody lists; the empty job (every member) and the empty profile (only the empty job); a skill repeated in a profile and in a job; all versus any. Hard: names differing in case and surrounding spaces; an opted-out member who would match; every member opted out. Very Hard: exactly min_count members (shown), one fewer (−1), a count of 0 (−1), and an opt-out that pushes a job below the minimum.

Common mistakes. Any-of instead of all-of; counting a member twice for a duplicate skill; requiring a repeated job skill twice; normalising only one side; subtracting opted-out members from a count that never included them, or counting them; building bitsets with x |= 1 << i per member (quadratic); returning 0 instead of −1 under the minimum.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Dense bitsets are 900M / 8 ≈ 112 MB per skill; use compressed bitmaps, shard members, and keep the dense form only for the most common skills. (2) Count per member how many of the job's skills they have (sum over posting lists in a counter, or bit-sliced addition across bitsets) and threshold. (3) Map free text to a canonical skill id at ingest, apply implication edges by expanding the profile's skills, and version the taxonomy so counts can be recomputed under one version. (4) Round or add noise to counts, rate-limit near-duplicate queries per account, and consider differential privacy for published aggregates.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct brute force that fails the timing check, or an index with all/any or duplicate errors. 3: correct and fast at the level attempted, with the sentinel. 4: also handles scale, threshold queries and differencing risks credibly.

import heapq


def salary_medians(events, k, lo=None, hi=None):
    # Hard and above compare trimmed, case-insensitive keys; at Medium every key is already
    # canonical, so normalising there changes nothing.
    key_of = lambda title, city: (title.strip().lower(), city.strip().lower())
    groups = {}   # key -> [low max-heap of (-salary, -idx), high min-heap of (salary, idx), n_low, n_high, gone]
    live = {}     # add index -> salary, for accepted reports not yet removed
    out = []

    def prune(g):
        low, high, gone = g[0], g[1], g[4]
        while low and -low[0][1] in gone:
            gone.discard(-heapq.heappop(low)[1])
        while high and high[0][1] in gone:
            gone.discard(heapq.heappop(high)[1])

    def balance(g):

def learning_path(target, courses, known=None):
    have = set(known or ())
    need = sorted(set(target) - have)
    k = len(need)
    bit = {s: 1 << i for i, s in enumerate(need)}
    best_by_mask = {}                    # distinct useful skill masks -> fewest minutes
    for _cid, minutes, skills in courses:
        m = 0
        for s in skills:
            m |= bit.get(s, 0)
        if m and (m not in best_by_mask or minutes < best_by_mask[m]):
            best_by_mask[m] = minutes
    full = (1 << k) - 1
    cover = 0
    for m in best_by_mask:
        cover |= m
    if cover != full:
        return None
    SHIFT = 40                            # key = courses * 2^40 + minutes
    INF = 1 << 62
    dp = [INF] * (full + 1)
    dp[0] = 0
    opts = [(m, (1 << SHIFT) + w) for m, w in best_by_mask.items()]
    for mask in range(full + 1):
        v = dp[mask]
        if v == INF or mask == full:
            continue
        for m, w in opts:
            nm = mask | m
            if nm != mask:
                c = v + w
                if c < dp[nm]:
                    dp[nm] = c
    v = dp[full]
    return (v >> SHIFT, v & ((1 << SHIFT) - 1))

Explanation. Only the skills still needed matter, so remove known and duplicates first and number the rest. Each course becomes a bitmask of the needed skills it teaches; a course with an empty mask can never help and is dropped, and among courses with the same mask only the shortest can be in a best plan. dp[mask] is the best (courses, minutes) for a plan that teaches at least mask, packed into one integer (courses · 2⁴⁰ + minutes) so that one comparison orders by courses first and minutes second. Masks are processed in increasing order: every transition mask → mask | m goes to a larger mask (or stays put and is skipped), so each state is final when it is read. If the union of all course masks is not the full mask, some needed skill is taught nowhere and the answer is None. An empty set of needed skills gives (0, 0).

def former_colleagues(positions, min_days, today, opted_out=None):
    skip = set(opted_out or ())
    stints = {}                              # (member, company) -> [start, end]
    for member, company, start, end in positions:
        if member in skip:
            continue
        if end is None:
            end = today
        s = stints.get((member, company))
        if s is None:
            stints[(member, company)] = [start, end]
        else:                                # a promotion: same stint, wider span
            if start < s[0]:
                s[0] = start
            if end > s[1]:
                s[1] = end
    out = {}
    by_company = {}
    for (member, company), (start, end) in stints.items():
        out.setdefault(member, {})[company] = 0
        if end - start + 1 >= min_days:      # shorter stints can never qualify
            by_company.setdefault(company, []).append((member, start, end - min_days + 1))
    # Overlap >= D  <=>  the shrunken intervals [start, end - D + 1] intersect.
    for company, rows in by_company.items():
        lo = sorted(a for _, a, _ in rows)
        hi = sorted(b for _, _, b in rows)
        for member, a, b in rows:
            out[member][company] = bisect_right(lo, b) - bisect_left(hi, a) - 1
    return out

Every remaining member gets an entry with 0 for each of their companies. Overlap of two inclusive intervals is min(e₁, e₂) − max(s₁, s₂) + 1, and overlap ≥ D is the same as all four of e₁ − s₁, e₂ − s₂, e₁ − s₂ and e₂ − s₁ being at least D − 1. The first two say both stints last at least D days; a shorter stint never qualifies. For the others, the remaining two say that the shrunken intervals [s, e − D + 1] intersect. Two intervals intersect when one starts at or before the other's end and ends at or after the other's start. For stint i with shrunken [a, b], the stints that start at or before b include every intersecting one plus those that end before a, and every interval ending before a also starts before b. So the count is #(starts ≤ b) − #(ends < a) − 1 (minus itself), found with two sorted arrays and bisect.

from datetime import date, timedelta

EPOCH = date(1970, 1, 1)


def creator_report(creator, offset_min, posts, events, deleted):
    deleted = set(deleted)
    rows = {}                                   # (day, post) -> [views, unique, reactions]
    seen = set()                                # (day, post, member) for unique viewers
    for ev in events:
        member = ev["member"]
        if member in deleted or member == creator:          # deletion honoured everywhere
            continue
        base = ev["post"].split("#")[0]                       # an edit keeps the post's identity
        post = posts.get(base)
        if post is None:
            continue
        original = post["reshare_of"] or base                 # a reshare is credited to the original
        if posts[original]["author"] != creator:
            continue
        day = (EPOCH + timedelta(days=(ev["ts"] + offset_min * 60) // 86400)).isoformat()
        row = rows.setdefault((day, original), [0, 0, 0])
        if ev["type"] == "view":
            row[0] += 1
            if (day, original, member) not in seen:         # unique per post and local day
                seen.add((day, original, member))
                row[1] += 1
        elif ev["type"] == "react":
            row[2] += 1
    return [[day, post, v, u, r] for (day, post), (v, u, r) in sorted(rows.items())]

Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Saved-search store and index. Saved searches are rows (search_id, member_id, filters, cadence, channel, created_at, active) in a key-value store, plus an inverted index from each search's most selective required field to search ids: normalised title, location (or "remote"), company. A search with a title and a location is indexed under one key (for example title|location), so a posting with title T in city C looks up T|C, T|remote and the company key, and gets a small candidate set. Remaining filters (seniority, salary floor, keywords) are checked on the candidates. Searches with no selective field go into a small "broad" bucket evaluated by a separate, batched path.
  • Matching. New, edited and closed postings arrive as events. A stream processor partitioned by posting id looks up candidates, checks filters, calls the given scoring function, and emits (member_id, posting_id, search_id, score, matched_at) to a match topic partitioned by member id. Postings that match a very large share of searches are expanded in batches with back-pressure.
  • Per-member queues and scheduler. A consumer keyed by member keeps pending matches per member (deduplicated by posting id). At each member's send time (instant, daily or weekly cadence, outside quiet hours), it reads the member's current notification settings and unsubscribes, revalidates every pending posting (still open, still matching after edits, not already alerted), ranks by score, applies the cap ({{cap}}), and sends.
  • Delivery and idempotency. An alerted(member_id, posting_id) table is the source of truth, written in the same transaction as the outbox record for the message; the sender reads the outbox and uses the message id as an idempotency key with the email or push provider. Retention of alerted is at least the posting's lifetime.
  • Measurement. A small random holdout of matches (for example 5%, by hash of member and posting) is recorded but not sent. Applications within {{attribution_window}} of the alert, or of the would-be alert time for held-out matches, are compared between groups, by cadence and channel, as aggregates with confidence intervals. The difference is the alert's effect; raw "alerted members apply 3× more" is selection.

Competing designs to accept. Batch matching every hour with a join of new postings to searches on the indexed keys (simpler, less fresh; accept if the cadence is digest-first); a search engine with percolator-style stored queries for matching; per-member pull at send time ("run my saved searches against postings since my last alert") for digest cadences, which avoids fan-out but costs one query per member per period. Each is fine with the trade-off explained.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Fan-out from broad postings; hot member queues for members with many searches; caps enforced at match time (then settings changed later are ignored); duplicate sends after crashes; sending alerts for closed postings; measurement confounded by selection; inactive searches costing most of the matching work.

Incident guidance.

  • 30 000 near-identical postings in ten minutes: matching fan-out explodes. Collapse near-duplicates from one employer into one alert candidate per member (keyed by employer and normalised title), rate-limit the employer's postings in the matcher, and rely on per-member deduplication and caps so each member hears once. Watch match-topic lag; other employers' postings should keep flowing on their partitions.
  • Delivery worker crashes after sending, before recording: with an outbox written before sending and provider idempotency keys, the restart resends with the same keys and the provider drops duplicates; without them, members get duplicates. Reconcile with the provider's delivery log, and fix by recording the intent first.
  • A posting closes after matching, while queued for members who get at most {{cap}}: revalidation at send time drops it from every pending queue; nothing is sent. If digests were already rendered, re-render or skip the item, and track "closed before send" as a metric.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The posting's candidate set is huge; the matcher expands it in batches, member queues absorb it, caps limit what is sent, and ranking decides whether this posting makes each member's cut. (2) Re-match edited postings; searches that now match get new candidates; searches that no longer match drop the pending item; the digest shows the current salary. (3) alerted(member, posting) checked at send time across channels, written with the outbox. (4) Selection: members with saved searches are active job seekers. Report the holdout difference (incremental applications per thousand alerts). (5) Pause alerts for long-inactive searches after notifying the member, measure re-engagement on a holdout first, and stop matching paused searches.

Rubric anchors. 2: scans all searches per posting; caps at match time; no deduplication or measurement design. 3: inverted index on selective fields, matching separated from delivery, per-member queues with caps and settings at send time, idempotent sends, revalidation of closed postings. 4: also handles broad-posting fan-out, measures with a holdout reported as aggregates, and gives a specific plan for each incident.

Strong signals. Asks which filters are required versus optional before choosing the index key; brings up the holdout unprompted. Red flags. Inferring job-seeking status for members who did not save a search; reporting individual members' applications to anyone; "send everything and let the member unsubscribe".

LNK-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Events. The player sends (learner_id, device_id, video_id, session_id, seq, watched_intervals, position, event_time, licence_context) in batches; the server adds received_time. A batch is identified by (device_id, session_id, seq), so retries are recognised and dropped. Events land immutably in an append-only log.
  • Merged progress. Per learner and video, the state is the union of watched intervals (a sorted list of disjoint intervals) plus the resume position from the session with the latest event_time, tie-broken by device and sequence. Union is commutative, associative and idempotent, so late, duplicate and out-of-order uploads converge to the same state. Watched share is the union length over the video's length. Device clock skew affects only the resume choice, which is bounded by rejecting event times far in the future relative to received_time.
  • Completion and certificates. A completion evaluator runs when a learner's merged state changes, checks the completion rule (the learner {{completion_rule}}), and writes completion(learner_id, course_id, completed_at) with a unique key; the certificate is issued from that row by an idempotent job (the unique key makes concurrent runs harmless). Certificates are never revoked by late events; a later correction is a separate, audited decision with the learner told.
  • Licence context. At ingestion each event is tagged with the licence it happened under (from the learner's active licence assignment for that course), so employer reports select by licence id and never infer. Personal-interest learning carries no employer licence.
  • Employer reports. Built from licence-tagged state only: seats used, courses started and completed, pass/fail and dates where the licence terms allow. Reports for {{employer_seats}} seats are per licence; after the licence ends, identities follow the licence terms and deletion requests, and aggregates for the licence period may remain.
  • Learner view. "Continue where you left off" reads the merged resume position; progress bars read watched share. Both are the learner's own data.
  • Deletion and licence end. A deletion request removes the learner's events, merged state, completions and report rows (with recomputation of aggregates or suppression under a minimum group size), and is logged as done. Licence end stops new events being tagged to the licence at the cut-off, and reports generated after it reflect the terms.

Competing designs to accept. Storing raw intervals and computing progress on read for small scales; a streaming state store keyed by (learner, video) with periodic compaction to a table; keeping only furthest-position plus a watched bitmap of fixed-length segments (for example 5-second buckets), which is compact and also idempotent. Accept any where merges are order-independent and licence context is explicit.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Last-write-wins by upload time sending learners backwards; max-position marking skipped videos as watched; interval lists that grow without compaction; double certificates from concurrent evaluators; employer reports that include personal learning because context was inferred at report time; deletion that misses derived aggregates.

Incident guidance.

  • A week of held offline progress arrives in a day, out of order: the merge is order-independent, so state converges; the risk is load. Scale the consumers, process by learner partition, and expect a burst of completions and certificates, which must be idempotent. Monitor upload lag by app version.
  • A licence for {{employer_seats}} seats ends at midnight and the admin exports at 00:05: the report must reflect the licence's end rules. Events after the cut-off are not tagged to the licence; the export shows the licence period. Make the cut-off time explicit (time zone) and log what the export contained.
  • Double-counted seconds marked 4% of learners complete wrongly: with intervals, double counting cannot happen; with counters it can. Fix the computation, recompute completions from merged state, and decide with the product and legal owners what happens to certificates already issued; the learner is told plainly, and employer reports are corrected with a note.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Union of intervals: the learner's progress only grows; resume follows the latest session by event time, so the laptop's later session keeps the resume point. (2) Do not silently revoke; flag, recompute, and follow a documented correction policy with the learner informed. (3) Show "not started" for assigned learners under the licence, and nothing about personal learning or quiz answers beyond the terms. (4) Delete raw events, merged state and report rows, recompute aggregates, and keep a deletion log; certificates the learner shared publicly are removed from the profile. (5) Compact interval lists (merge adjacent intervals, cap fragmentation), or switch to fixed-length segment bitmaps per video.

Rubric anchors. 2: last-write-wins progress; furthest position as watched; licence inferred at report time. 3: idempotent uploads, interval union merge, resume by event time, exactly-once certificates, licence-tagged reports. 4: also handles clock skew, deletion through every output, licence-end semantics, compaction at scale, and a clear plan for each incident.

Strong signals. Separates "where to resume" from "what was watched" immediately; asks what the licence terms allow the employer to see. Red flags. Giving employers all of a learner's activity on the account; treating deletion as a flag that reports ignore.

LNK-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Entities. members (member_id, created_at, status active|closed, closed_at). One table per entry kind, each row a version of an entry with a stable entry_id:
    • position_versions (entry_id, member_id, version_no, title, company_page_id NULL, company_text NULL, start_month, end_month NULL, description, valid_from_month, valid_to_month, recorded_from, recorded_to, client_edit_seq, op insert|update|delete).
    • education_versions, skill_versions (entry_id, member_id, skill_id NULL, skill_text, …) and headline_versions, location_versions with the same recorded-time columns.
    • section_visibility_versions (member_id, section, audience everyone|connections|only_me, recorded_from, recorded_to).
  • Two time axes. Valid time is the business fact (the job ran from start_month to end_month); recorded time is when the system held this version. "What did the profile say at T" filters recorded_from <= T < recorded_to; "where did they work in month M, as known now" filters current versions (recorded_to = ∞) on start_month <= M <= COALESCE(end_month, M). A position added today with a 2019 start month has recorded_from = today and valid time from 2019.
  • Ordering edits. Versions are ordered by a per-entry sequence (server-assigned on accept, or a client sequence checked by the server), never by arrival; a stale edit is rejected or recorded as a conflict, not made current.
  • Visibility. Applied at read time from the current visibility version for every reader except the member. Point-in-time features for the matching model use only sections visible to that consumer under current settings (stricter of then and now is also acceptable if argued).
  • Applications. applications (application_id, member_id, posting_id, submitted_at) with application_profile_copy (application_id, payload) written once at submission; it is part of the application record and follows the application's retention.
  • Point-in-time features. For each (member, application_date): the versions with recorded_from <= application_date < recorded_to — recorded time, not valid time, or a correction made later leaks into training.
  • Erasure. Deletion of an entry or account closure writes an erasure request (member_id, entry_id NULL, requested_at, due_at = requested_at + {{erase_days}} days). Every store that holds profile-derived rows is registered with a delete path keyed by member_id/entry_id: versioned tables (row deletes or delete vectors, then compaction), snapshots and extracts (registered, partitioned or bucketed by member hash so one rewrite touches few files), caches (TTL below the window or explicit purge), and, as an alternative, per-member encryption keys destroyed on erasure (crypto-shredding). A completion check queries each registered store for the member before closing the request.
  • Retention. Non-current versions older than {{history_days}} days are purged by the same mechanism.
  • Aggregates. agg_skill_region_month (skill_id, region, month, members) computed from current versions at month-end with a minimum-member threshold; published cells stay as published (this exercise's rule), later months exclude erased data, and the method note says so.

Competing designs to accept. An event log of profile edits as the source of truth with versioned tables as projections, if erasure reaches the log (log compaction by key or per-member encryption). A full-profile document per version, if it is clear how per-skill questions are answered (an extracted entry table) and how erasure works. Uni-temporal versions plus an audit table, if both example questions can still be answered precisely.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Overwriting entries (no history); a single "effective date" column that mixes valid and recorded time; ordering versions by arrival; daily full-profile snapshots at {{members}} profiles (storage, and erasure must rewrite every snapshot); unregistered copies (extracts, notebooks, caches) that erasure cannot find; point-in-time features filtered on valid time (leakage); inferring protected traits from names, photos or dates.

Incident guidance.

  • Headline still in a training extract {{erase_days}} days after closure: contain by deleting the extract or the member's rows in it and pausing jobs that read it; fix by registering every materialised extract with the erasure service (a store that is not registered cannot be created by the pipeline tooling); guard with a completion check that scans every registered store for erased member ids before an erasure is marked done, plus an alert when a request nears its due date.
  • Résumé import wrote the upload month as start month: it confused recorded time with valid time. Contain by labelling the hiring-trends chart and pulling it; correct by re-importing with parsed start months (new versions, not overwrites) or flagging the batch as "start month unknown"; guard with a distribution check on start months per import batch and a rule that bulk imports never default valid time to the import date.
  • Out-of-order edits made an old title current: ordering by arrival time. Reorder affected entries by the per-entry sequence, write corrective versions, and tell affected applicants' employers only if the policy requires (application copies are what was sent); guard with server-side sequence checks that reject stale edits and a test that replays retried edits.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Version 1: recorded today, valid from three years ago; version 2 next week with the corrected title; deletion closes the entry and erasure removes both versions within {{erase_days}} days — before that only the member sees the history, after it nobody does; an application submitted in between keeps its own copy. (2) A join of (member_id, application_date) to versions with recorded_from <= application_date AND application_date < recorded_to. (3) Delete vectors or row-level deletes plus scheduled compaction, member-hash bucketing so a delete touches few files, or per-member keys. (4) Grain: (skill, region, month) over current versions at month-end; next month excludes deleted skills; last month's published cell stays and the note explains why. (5) Entry versions store only what changed; snapshots copy everything daily and make erasure touch every snapshot — entry versions are the strong answer, with an optional periodic snapshot for fast reads.

Rubric anchors. 2: a profile table overwritten in place, or a daily snapshot with a deleted flag. 3: entry versions with stable ids, valid and recorded time distinguished, an erasure path for the main tables. 4: also edit ordering, application copies, point-in-time features on recorded time, erasure that reaches snapshots, extracts and caches with a completion check, and an aggregate restatement policy.

Strong signals. Separates "true when" from "known when" without prompting; treats erasure as a property of every derived store. Red flags. "Soft delete is enough"; inferring age or gender from graduation dates or names; using hidden sections for features.

LNK-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Identities.
    • openings (opening_id, employer_id, requisition_id NULL, first_posted_at, status open|filled|cancelled, identity_method requisition|matched).
    • postings (posting_id, opening_id, employer_id, source direct|ats_feed, source_ref, posted_at, closed_at NULL, close_reason poster|auto_{{auto_close_days}}d|filled|ats_removed NULL); reopenings as posting_status_events (posting_id, status, at).
    • posting_versions (posting_id, version_no, title, location, workplace_type, salary_min, salary_max, currency, pay_period, valid_from, valid_to).
  • Repost identity. With a requisition id: opening = (employer, requisition). Without: a deterministic matcher (same employer, normalised title, location, overlapping or adjacent posting windows within N days) that assigns identity_method = matched and a confidence; a labelled sample of pairs measures precision and recall each quarter.
  • Applications. applications (application_id, member_id, posting_id, posting_version_no, submitted_at, channel on_platform); offsite_clicks (click_id, member_id, posting_id, clicked_at) kept in a separate fact, never unioned into applications.
  • Status. application_stage_events (application_id, employer_stage_id, stage_version, at, actor) append-only; employer_stages (employer_id, stage_id, version, name, visible_status submitted|viewed|not_selected|NULL, valid_from, valid_to); applicant_status_shown (application_id, visible_status, shown_at, source_event_id) written when the applicant's view changes. "Not selected" is written only from an explicit employer action (this exercise's rule).
  • Facts. fct_applications_daily (posting_id, opening_id, date, applications); fct_application_snapshot (application_id, submitted_at, first_viewed_at, last_visible_status, received_any_status_after_submit, closed_reason) as an accumulating snapshot; fct_openings (opening_id, postings_count_90d, …) for repost counts.

Competing designs to accept. A single postings table with a nullable previous_posting_id chain instead of openings, if the matcher and its error rate are discussed. Event-sourced applications with materialised current status, if "what was shown" is an event, not recomputed from the current mapping. A canonical cross-employer stage taxonomy for reporting, if the applicant-visible mapping is still per employer and versioned.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Treating each posting as a job (reposts inflate counts and reset time-to-fill); status overwritten (history and what-was-shown lost); recomputing shown status from today's mapping; salary shown from the current version; offsite clicks counted as applications; closure reason missing; ATS feed ids treated as globally stable.

Incident guidance.

  • ATS migration re-sent postings with new ids: contain by pausing ingestion for that employer and suppressing the "new" flag; map new ids to old via (employer, requisition id or source_ref + title + location) and re-point the openings; keep applications on their original postings and show applicants an unchanged status; guard with a per-employer anomaly check (share of postings that are new versus a baseline, here about {{ats_share}} of a day's postings) that holds the batch for review.
  • "Not selected" sent after auto-sorting: roll back the mapping, and correct what applicants were shown (an apology status is a product decision; the data change is a new shown-status event, not a deletion); guard by requiring explicit employer action for "not selected", mapping changes reviewed before activation, and a canary that alerts when shown "not selected" volume jumps for one employer.
  • Auto-closed postings counted as filled: closure reason was missing. Backfill reasons from the auto-close job's log (closed at exactly posted_at + {{auto_close_days}} days with no poster action), restate time-to-fill with a note, and make close_reason NOT NULL with "unknown" never counted as filled.

Follow-up guidance. (1) One opening, posting v1 then v2 (salary edited; the first 40 applications keep v1), auto-close event, a new posting linked to the same opening, then filled; earlier applicants see "no longer accepting applications" on the closed posting and their own status as the employer moves them. (2) Matcher on employer + normalised title + location + time gap; measure with a labelled sample, and treat requisition ids as ground truth where present. (3) Stage versions keep the old mapping for events already shown; applicants already in the stage get a new shown status only if the employer's action changes it; last month's metric uses events as they were. (4) Report the share viewed within N days and the median among viewed; a month is final after N days plus lag. (5) Events and shown-status are append-only facts; the per-application snapshot is rebuilt for touched applications; "what was shown" is reproduced from the shown-status events.

Rubric anchors. 2: one jobs table and one applications table with a status column. 3: openings, postings, versions, status history and offsite clicks separated. 4: also a measured repost matcher, versioned stage mappings, what-was-shown as events, closure reasons, and each incident guarded.

Strong signals. Asks what the applicant actually saw and when; separates "we know they clicked" from "they applied". Red flags. Inferring rejections from silence; showing employer stage names to applicants; counting reposts as new demand.

LNK-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Identity. organisations (org_id, created_at); pages (page_id, org_id, created_at, retired_at NULL); page_names (page_id, name, handle, valid_from, valid_to) for rebrands (a rebrand is a new name version on the same page).
  • Merges. page_merges (merge_id, from_page_id, into_page_id, merged_at, unmerged_at NULL, verified_by). Resolution follows active merges to a fixed point; a cycle is rejected at write time (the merge service checks that into_page_id does not resolve to from_page_id). A materialised page_resolution (page_id, resolved_page_id, valid_from, valid_to) closure table is rebuilt on each merge or unmerge, so a warehouse join is a single equi-join with a time condition.
  • Affiliation. page_affiliations (parent_page_id, child_page_id, kind subsidiary|acquired|showcase, valid_from, valid_to); an acquisition is an affiliation from its date; retiring the acquired page into the acquirer is a separate merge with its own date.
  • Positions. Member positions keep the company_page_id the member chose, or company_text; resolution happens at read time. company_text_links (normalised_text, country, page_id, linked_at, method, reviewed_by) links free text later, with evidence beyond the name.
  • Followers. follows (member_id, page_id, followed_at, unfollowed_at) on the original page id, so an unmerge can return followers to their own page. Follows created on the surviving page during a merge record via_merge_from when the follow came through a resolved link.
  • Insights. fct_page_headcount_week (resolved_page_id, week, function, location_band, members) built "as is" (current resolution) for the administrator's current view, with "as was" available for history; cells below {{insights_floor}} suppressed; published differences protected by rounding to a fixed base, a minimum reportable change, or calibrated noise, and suppression of complementary cells.

Competing designs to accept. Rewriting position links at merge time if a full undo log makes unmerges exact (costly, but defensible). A graph of pages and edges with time properties, if the closure table or equivalent makes resolution cheap. Differential privacy for insights, if the accuracy cost for small pages is discussed.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Rewriting positions and follows (unmerge impossible); chains and cycles followed row by row at warehouse scale; rebrands created as new pages; acquisitions merging history silently; suppression only per cell, leaving differences and complements to reveal small groups; fuzzy name matching across countries without review.

Incident guidance.

  • Differencing revealed a group below {{insights_floor}}: contain by withdrawing the affected function table for that page; fix by protecting differences (round counts to a base, require changes of at least the floor before they show, or add noise) and suppressing complementary cells; guard with an automated check that computes week-over-week and merge-before/after differences for every published table and blocks publication when any difference is below the floor.
  • Rebrand entered as a new page: merge the new page into the original with an effective time and convert it to a name version, so positions resolve to one page; re-run headcount for the period with a note; guard with a duplicate-page detector (same domain, overlapping administrators, similar names) that routes new pages to review.
  • Bad merge of two companies: unmerge; follows recorded with the original page id return automatically, and those created during the merge window go to the page whose link the member used (the via_merge_from trail), or are asked to re-follow; guard with stronger verification before merges (domain or administrator overlap) and a holding period during which merges can be undone without data loss.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Rows: A→B (t1), B→C (t2), A→B unmerged (t3). A position on A resolves to C between t2 and t3 and to A after t3; positions on B still resolve to C. (2) "As is" combines both companies across the whole period (a step-free line) and "as was" shows the step at the acquisition date; an administrator usually sees "as is" with a dated annotation. (3) Show the cell if both values are above the floor and the difference is published only if it meets the protection rule; never let an unmerge expose the small remainder. (4) Link with evidence (domain, location, reviewed), apply from the link date or restate with a note, never silently. (5) Materialise the closure table, rebuilt incrementally on each of the roughly {{merges_per_month}} monthly merges.

Rubric anchors. 2: positions rewritten to the surviving page, no history. 3: merge map with times, resolution at read time, affiliations with dates, the floor applied to cells. 4: also cycles and unmerges, the closure table, as-was versus as-is stated, difference attacks handled, and each incident guarded.

Strong signals. Treats unmerge as a first-class requirement; spots the differencing risk unprompted. Red flags. Listing individual employees in insights; inferring employment from anything but what members listed; deleting retired page ids.

LNK-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Ownership. customers (customer_id), contracts (contract_id, customer_id, starts_at, ends_at, delete_after = ends_at + {{retention_days}} days), seats (seat_id, contract_id), seat_assignments (seat_id, recruiter_member_id, valid_from, valid_to). Work is keyed by seat and contract, and attribution joins the event time to the seat assignment in force.
  • Projects. projects (project_id, contract_id, created_by_seat_id, created_at, closed_at); project_ownership (project_id, seat_id, valid_from, valid_to) for transfers.
  • Candidates in projects. project_candidates (project_id, candidate_member_id, added_at, added_by_seat_id) — a reference to the member, never a profile copy; the profile is read live under the candidate's current settings.
  • Stages. stage_definitions (contract_id, stage_id, version, name, sort_order, canonical_stage, valid_from, valid_to); stage_events (project_id, candidate_member_id, stage_id, stage_version, at, seat_id) append-only. Time in stage comes from consecutive events; reports group by canonical_stage (contacted, screen, interview, offer, hired), so renames and reorders of the {{custom_stages}} stages stay comparable.
  • Notes and messages. notes (note_id, contract_id, project_id, candidate_member_id, seat_id, body, created_at). threads (thread_id, contract_id, candidate_member_id, owner_seat_id); messages (message_id, thread_id, sender seat_id|candidate, sender_member_id, sent_at) — the sender of each message is fixed, the thread's owner seat changes on transfer.
  • Deletion. Every customer-owned row carries contract_id; a deletion job runs at delete_after for the contract and for every registered derived table and export. Candidate account closure removes the candidate from projects (references die with the profile); notes about a closed account are deleted at closure in the strict policy, or at contract end in the lenient one — either is acceptable if argued and stated to the customer.
  • Facts. fct_stage_reached (project_id, canonical_stage, candidate, first_reached_at, seat_id_at_time, recruiter_at_time); fct_thread_first_reply (thread_id, first_message_at, first_reply_at, seat_id_at_first_message); hires per recruiter from the seat assignment in force when the hire event happened.

Competing designs to accept. Ownership by recruiter with an explicit transfer table, if attribution is still by the holder at event time. A global canonical stage taxonomy instead of per-contract mapping. A per-customer database or schema (strong isolation, simpler deletion), if cross-customer analytics are kept aggregate.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Recruiter as owner (orphaned projects on departure); attribution by current seat holder; a current_stage column (no time in stage); stage reports by name or sort order; profile copies (stale, and erasure misses them); deletion that skips exports and derived tables; any cross-customer signal ("another company contacted this candidate").

Incident guidance.

  • Hires credited to the new seat holders: attribution read the current holder. Rebuild the fact by joining each stage event's time to seat_assignments; restate the report with a note; guard with a test that transfers a seat in a fixture and asserts last month's hires stay with the original recruiter.
  • Reordered stages reversed the conversion chart: the chart sorted by sort_order and grouped by stage name. Group by canonical stage, keep display order per stage version, and add a check that a stage-definition change producing a canonical-stage regression (e.g. offer before interview) requires administrator confirmation.
  • Export table missed by contract-end deletion: delete the export rows and stop the scheduled report; register every table and export with a contract_id in the deletion catalogue (an unregistered table cannot be created for customer data); prove completion with a post-deletion scan that every registered store has zero rows for the contract, {{retention_days}} days after the end date.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Events carry seat ids; the original recruiter is credited for the save, message and stages before departure, the new holder for the hire; replies during the {{transfer_lag_days}}-day gap belong to the thread, visible to administrators. (2) Canonical stages plus versioned definitions; time in stage from events. (3) The thread's owner seat is vacant; replies are stored and shown to the new holder after transfer; "replies per seat" attributes to the seat that sent the first message. (4) Delete projects, notes, stage events, threads' customer-side metadata and exports after {{retention_days}} days; aggregate usage counts without candidate identity may survive. (5) Within one contract, a per-candidate contact flag computed from that contract's threads only; never across contracts.

Rubric anchors. 2: recruiter-owned projects with a current stage column and profile copies. 3: seat-based ownership with assignment history, stage events, references not copies, contract-keyed deletion. 4: also canonical stages with versions, thread transfer semantics, attribution by holder at event time, candidate closure policy, cross-customer isolation and each incident guarded.

Strong signals. Says "the customer owns the work" first; attributes by time, not by current holder. Red flags. Copying profiles into projects; sharing contact history across customers; deleting history on transfer.

LNK-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{week_from}} and {{week_to}} are the instance's window)

WITH counted AS (                             -- self-views and closed accounts removed
  SELECT pv.viewed_id, pv.viewer_id, pv.viewed_at, m.time_zone,
         COALESCE((SELECT s.mode
                   FROM visibility_settings s
                   WHERE s.member_id = pv.viewer_id
                     AND s.effective_at <= pv.viewed_at
                   ORDER BY s.effective_at DESC
                   LIMIT 1), 'named') AS mode
  FROM profile_views pv
  JOIN members m ON m.member_id = pv.viewed_id          -- the viewed member's time zone
  JOIN members w ON w.member_id = pv.viewer_id
  WHERE pv.viewer_id <> pv.viewed_id
    AND w.closed_at IS NULL
), per_viewer AS (                            -- one row per (member, local week, viewer)
  SELECT viewed_id AS member_id,
         date_trunc('week', viewed_at AT TIME ZONE time_zone)::date AS week_start,
         viewer_id,
         bool_or(mode = 'named') AS named
  FROM counted
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
)
SELECT member_id, week_start,
       COUNT(*)                          AS viewers,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE named)     AS named_viewers,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT named) AS private_viewers
FROM per_viewer
WHERE week_start BETWEEN DATE '{{week_from}}' AND DATE '{{week_to}}'
GROUP BY member_id, week_start
ORDER BY member_id, week_start;

Explanation. Each view first gets the mode in force when it happened: the latest setting at or before viewed_at (a correlated subquery with ORDER BY … DESC LIMIT 1), defaulting to named when the viewer had no setting yet. Self-views and views by closed accounts are removed before anything is counted. The view is then placed in a week of the viewed member's time zone: viewed_at AT TIME ZONE time_zone turns the instant into local wall-clock time, and date_trunc('week', …) takes its Monday. Grouping by (member, week, viewer) collapses repeat views, and bool_or(mode = 'named') applies the rule that one named view makes a named viewer; the outer counts then add up by construction. The window is applied to the local week start, so the last week is included up to the end of its local Sunday.

Complexity. One pass over views, with an index probe on visibility_settings (member_id, effective_at) per view (the primary key serves it), then two hash aggregates. At production scale the setting in force is better attached once, when the view event is recorded, or with a range join on setting intervals (effective_at to the next effective_at) instead of a probe per view.

Dialect notes. The correlated LIMIT 1 subquery is not allowed in BigQuery or Spark SQL; there, build setting intervals with LEAD(effective_at) OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY effective_at) and join on effective_at <= viewed_at AND viewed_at < next_effective_at, or use an as-of join where the engine has one (Snowflake ASOF JOIN … MATCH_CONDITION (viewed_at >= effective_at)). bool_or is BOOLOR_AGG in Snowflake, LOGICAL_OR in BigQuery, bool_or or max in Spark; COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) becomes COUNT_IF (Snowflake, BigQuery, Spark) or SUM(CASE …) (MySQL). Time zones: CONVERT_TIMEZONE('UTC', time_zone, viewed_at) (Snowflake), DATETIME(viewed_at, time_zone) (BigQuery), from_utc_timestamp (Spark), CONVERT_TZ (MySQL, which needs the zone tables loaded). Week truncation: DATE_TRUNC('WEEK', …) is Monday-based in Snowflake by default (session parameter WEEK_START) and in Spark; in BigQuery use DATE_TRUNC(d, WEEK(MONDAY)), because plain WEEK starts on Sunday. None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. A self-view; repeat views by one viewer in one week; a viewer who switched from named to private mid-week and viewed before and after (counts once, as named); a viewer whose setting was private at the time and changed to named only after the data; a viewer whose first setting comes after their view (default named); viewers who never changed a setting. Hard adds a closed account with views in the window (and sometimes a second), a setting that took effect at exactly the second of a view, views exactly at the local Monday 00:00 that opens the window, at the last second of its final Sunday and at the Monday 00:00 after it, and European zones across the 2026-10-25 clock change. Very Hard adds members on several continents with views that are Monday in UTC but Sunday locally (west of UTC) and the reverse (east of UTC), across both the European and North American clock changes.

Common mistakes. Counting self-views; counting views instead of viewers; counting a mixed-mode viewer in both columns, or as private; using the viewer's current (latest) setting for past views; an inner join or a NULL filter that drops viewers with no setting yet; excluding the last week of the window; (Hard+) a strict < that misses a setting effective at the exact second; counting closed accounts; truncating weeks in UTC; (Very Hard) using the viewer's time zone. Each has a diagnostic. A plain LEFT JOIN visibility_settings on member_id without picking one row multiplies views by the number of settings, which inflates the view counts but, because of the distinct counting, often hides as a mode error.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Attach the mode when the view is recorded and keep per (member, week) the set of viewer ids with a named flag (or a per-week viewer table); a closure then deletes that viewer's rows and the week's counts are recomputed from the remaining rows, rather than decremented from a stored count. (2) Either is defensible if stated: re-bucket all weeks in the new zone (consistent, but past numbers move) or freeze past weeks; members generally expect stable past numbers with a note. (3) A small private count can identify a person when combined with outside knowledge; options include showing "a few private viewers" below a threshold or only showing private views in aggregate across weeks — the strong answer names the trade-off with the member's legitimate interest. (4) It exposes viewers who chose privacy: roll back immediately, purge caches, treat as a privacy incident with notification per policy; a test with a viewer who switched modes would have caught it.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but the current setting or counted views, or weeks in UTC. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains how to precompute safely with closures, the time-zone change policy, and the small-count disclosure risk.

Strong signals. Asks which time zone owns the week, and what happens at the exact second of a switch; collapses to viewers before counting. Red flags. Using the latest setting for history (a privacy failure, not only a wrong number); joining all settings and then SELECT DISTINCT; exposing any per-viewer detail beyond what the member's own page shows.
LNK-L3-05.reference_sql:
WITH counted AS (                             -- self-views and closed accounts removed
  SELECT pv.viewed_id, pv.viewer_id, pv.viewed_at, m.time_zone,
         COALESCE((SELECT s.mode
                   FROM visibility_settings s
                   WHERE s.member_id = pv.viewer_id
                     AND s.effective_at <= pv.viewed_at
                   ORDER BY s.effective_at DESC
                   LIMIT 1), 'named') AS mode
  FROM profile_views pv
  JOIN members m ON m.member_id = pv.viewed_id          -- the viewed member's time zone
  JOIN members w ON w.member_id = pv.viewer_id
  WHERE pv.viewer_id <> pv.viewed_id
    AND w.closed_at IS NULL
), per_viewer AS (                            -- one row per (member, local week, viewer)
  SELECT viewed_id AS member_id,
         date_trunc('week', viewed_at AT TIME ZONE time_zone)::date AS week_start,
         viewer_id,
         bool_or(mode = 'named') AS named
  FROM counted
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
)
SELECT member_id, week_start,
       COUNT(*)                          AS viewers,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE named)     AS named_viewers,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT named) AS private_viewers
FROM per_viewer
WHERE week_start BETWEEN DATE '{{week_from}}' AND DATE '{{week_to}}'
GROUP BY member_id, week_start
